approach: A scoping review methodology was used to select and synthesize preclinical and human studies. Studies were included if they assessed sleep/circadian disruption, gut microbiome outcomes, and at least one functional biomarker (hormones, metabolites, neurotransmitters, or inflammation). Data were stratified by sample type (plasma/serum, GI tissue, brain tissue, etc.) and categorized using hierarchical databases (HMDB, KEGG, LIPID MAPS). Results were grouped by intervention type (sleep disruption vs. circadian disruption) and biomarker class to identify convergent functional signatures.

contribution_and_limits.limits: Most included studies are observational or cross-sectional, limiting causal inference. Human data are sparse and heterogeneous. The review does not establish direct causal mediation by specific taxa but rather associations. Specific mechanisms like kynurenine pathway metabolites were noted as under-measured in current literature.

key_findings.finding: Increased HPA axis activity (CRH, ACTH, cortisol/corticosterone); decreased GABA, serotonin, melatonin; increased pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α); decreased fecal SCFAs; downregulated amino acid and lipid metabolism; upregulated glycolysis/TCA cycle.
Increased primary bile acids and decreased secondary bile acids; increased LPS biosynthesis and bacterial virulence pathways; localized GI inflammation (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-17).

Limited data; generally paralleled preclinical inflammatory responses (increased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, LPS); decreased fecal SCFAs associated with poor sleep quality/short duration; conflicting cortisol responses compared to rodents.

problem_or_question: To synthesize evidence on how sleep and circadian disruption affect not just the composition but the functional capacity of the gut microbiome and host physiology, specifically identifying mechanistic pathways (neuroendocrine, immune, metabolic) that link these systems.
research_scope: The review synthesizes preclinical (rodent) and translational (human) studies examining the bidirectional relationship between sleep/circadian disruption and the gut microbiome. It focuses on functional biomarkers—hormones, neurotransmitters, inflammatory mediators, metabolites, and functional genes—in addition to microbial composition.
work_summary: This scoping review (Part II of a series) integrates findings from 83 studies (59 rodent, 24 human) that measured functional biomarkers alongside sleep/microbiome outcomes. It identifies consistent mechanistic links between sleep disruption and host homeostasis changes mediated by the microbiome, including HPA axis activation, altered bile acid metabolism, inflammation-related shifts, and disrupted tryptophan pathways. The authors argue that while taxonomic responses vary, functional signatures converge, suggesting metabolic and signaling biomarkers are more stable indicators of microbiome involvement in sleep pathology than composition alone.
